heading: A service that needs another service: Tac
body:
A service can need another service. Mark a field with Needs and give it the type of the other service. The field holds the same instance that the page uses. The view below shows {counter.count}, and TallyService changes that count when it calls increment on its counter field. So a click on Bump changes both lines. In JavaScript and TypeScript, the field name is the instance name of the other service: counter for CounterService.

In Go, `// @Needs` sits on the line above a field such as `counter *CounterService` (ADR 0045). All Go services of a page build into one Go package, so TallyService names CounterService without an import and calls its methods directly. The field holds a pointer, so TallyService and the page share one CounterService. The field stays inside the service: the page never reads it. Tachyon creates the needed service first and runs its OnStart first, so the OnStart of TallyService can already use counter. When TallyService calls counter.Increment() and CounterService publishes an event there, the event reaches every listener on the page, as if the page had called the method. Tachyon stops the services in the opposite order: OnStop of TallyService runs before OnStop of CounterService. If the page disposes of its CounterService first, TallyService keeps it until TallyService stops. The OnEvent methods of a needed Go service run when the page uses that service too, as this view does with counter.

A needed Go service is a page singleton: it keeps its state when the components that use it come and go, and it stops when the last Go service of the page is disposed. The build refuses these Go fields with TY1406, at the field: a field that holds the service by value, such as `counter CounterService`, because a copy is not shared; a field whose service has one instance for each component, because it is Lifetime prototype or NeedsAll; services that need each other in a circle, which you break with an event; and a field whose type the page has under two instance names, unless the field name is one of them.

Python writes the marker inside the field's type: `counter: Annotated[CounterService, needs]`. The field holds the CounterService that the page uses, so it is never a property of the component. A Dart service takes no Needs marker here. TallyService declares `late CounterService counter;`, a field typed with the other Dart service and named after its instance, and the page fills it with that same instance (ADR 0033). With `@Needs` on that field, the build stops with TY1009, because Needs in Dart builds a collaborator class from the service's own file. A C++ service needs another C++ service with `[[Needs]] CounterService& counter;`. Every C++ service of a page program is one shared instance, and Tachyon compiles CounterService before TallyService (ADR 0099).

An F# service needs another F# service with a Needs property: `[<Needs>]` above `member val Counter : CounterService = Unchecked.defaultof<CounterService> with get, set`. A primary constructor parameter, such as `type TallyService(counter: CounterService) =`, works too. The property holds the CounterService that the page uses, and the page never sees it. As in Go, Tachyon starts CounterService first, and TallyService always stops before CounterService. CounterService keeps its state while the components that use it come and go, and it stops when the last F# service of the page is disposed. When the property type is a base service, such as `GreeterService`, and `LoudGreeterService` inherits it, `[<Named("LoudGreeterService")>]` under `[<Needs>]` picks the F# service that fills it, as in C++. The build refuses with TY1406 a needed service that has one instance for each component, and services that need each other in a circle. It refuses a Needs property whose type is a C# service with TY1405. For a browser resource such as Clock, F# takes no Needs: write `let clock = Clock()`.

A Java service needs another Java service with `@Needs` above a field such as `private final CounterService counter;` (ADR 0083). A Java service file may name another Java service class of the page, in `extends`, a field or a local variable, and the build qualifies the name, so TallyService names CounterService without an import. The field holds the page's own CounterService, so TallyService and the page share one instance, and the field stays inside the service because it is private. As in Go, the needed service runs its OnStart before the service that needs it, events that it publishes go out through the component whose call is running, and it runs OnStop only after the last holder lets go; when no component holds anything any more, it stops. A field gets the service of its exact class. With a base service GreeterService and a subclass service `LoudGreeterService extends GreeterService`, the field `@Needs private final GreeterService greeter;` gets GreeterService, and `@Named("LoudGreeterService")` on its own line under `@Needs` gives the same field the subclass. Named takes the class name of a Java service of the page, and each annotation goes on its own line. The shared type is a base service, because a Java models file refuses an interface. When the page has two instances of one service class, the field name picks the instance. The build refuses these Java fields with TY1406, at the field: a needed service that is Lifetime prototype or NeedsAll, because it has one instance for each component and a field cannot name one; a field that cannot tell which provider it means, because several services fit and the field name matches none of them; services that need each other in a circle, which you break with an event (publish it, and handle it with OnEvent); and a Named that names no Java service of the page.

The other Tac languages have no tab here, because their browser services cannot need another service yet. The build refuses the field in Rust, Kotlin and Swift with TY1406, at the field and before the language's compiler runs, and in C# with TY1308: Needs there takes only the providers that the language's browser build supplies, such as a client or a browser resource. A Rust field would hold its own copy of CounterService instead of the page's, whether it holds `Arc<CounterService>` or the service by value, and so would a parameter of `fn new`. Kotlin and Swift build each browser service on its own, so the page has no CounterService to fill the field with. In Ruby and Lua, the build refuses a Needs field whose type is another service with TY2015, at the field: `#[Needs]` with `# @return [CounterService]` on `attr_reader :counter` in Ruby (ADR 0054), and `-- @Needs` with `---@type CounterService` on `counter = nil,` in Lua (ADR 0085). In these languages Needs takes a Store, a Converter, a Helper, an HTTPClient or a browser API such as `Clock` or `Clipboard` in Ruby, and a Converter in Lua. A Ruby `#[Needs]` field also needs its `# @return [Type]` comment: without one the page cannot fill the field, and the build stops with TY2015 at the field. To reach CounterService from Ruby or Lua, let the view call it, or publish an event that CounterService handles with OnEvent. Injection: Tac above shows Needs with helpers, and One per page, or one per component explains Lifetime.
